items.e: A dying man is regarded as a living entity in respect of all matters in the world: he holds [his brother’s wife] tied to the leviratical marriage, he frees [his mother] from the obligation of a leviratical marriage and enables her to eat terumah , and he [may also] disqualify her from eating terumah; he inherits and transmits; if one of his limbs is severed, it is regarded as a limb cut off from the living; if [part of his] flesh [is severed], it is regarded as flesh cut off from the living; and the blood of his sin-offering and guilt-offering is sprinkled for him until the time he dies.

We do not tie up his cheek-bones, or stop up his apertures, or place a metal vessel or anything which chills on his navel; as it is stated, Before the silver cord is snapped asunder and the golden bowl is shattered, and the pitcher is broken at the fountain.
We may not move him, or place him on sand or salt until he dies.

We may not close the eyes of a dying man. Whoever touches and moves him is a murderer. For R. Meir used to say: He can be compared to a lamp which is dripping; should a man touch it he extinguishes it. Similarly whoever closes the eyes of a dying man is considered as if he had taken his life.
We do not rend the garments or bare the shoulder, or deliver a memorial address, or bring the coffin into the house until he dies.
We do not summon the people or recount his good deeds. R. Judah said: If he is a scholar we recount his good deeds.

In the town people do not greet each other. This applies only in a village, but in a large city it is permissible. We do not carry out the mourning rites for one who came out [at birth] by pieces or with feet foremost, or for one born prematurely at eight months alive or at nine months dead.

For a non-Jew or a slave we do not occupy ourselves with his funeral rites, but we exclaim of him, ‘Alas lion! alas mighty man!’. R. Judah said: [We, for instance, exclaim], ‘Alas, Ṭabi! alas, faithful man who ate of his labour!’. They said to him, ‘[If so], what have you left [to be said] of worthy men [who are not slaves]?’ He replied, ‘If he was worthy, why should we not say it of him, since we do not receive condolence for [the loss of] male or female slaves?’

It is related that when R. Eliezer’s female slave died, his disciples came to comfort him. He entered the courtyard [to avoid them], but they followed him; he went into the house, but they followed him. He said to them, ‘I imagined that you would be scalded with tepid water, but now you are not even scalded with hot water. Have [the Sages] not said: We do not receive condolence for slaves because they are reckoned as animals?’

And when Ṭabi the slave of Rabban Gamaliel died, he received condolence for him. They asked him, ‘Master, have you not taught us that we do not receive condolence for slaves?’ He replied, ‘My slave Ṭabi was unlike all other slaves; he was a worthy man’.

He also permitted Ṭabi to put on the tefillin . They said to him, ‘Master, have you not taught us that slaves are exempt from [the precept of] tefillin? ’ He replied, ‘My slave Ṭabi was unlike all other slaves; he was a worthy man’.
We do not call male and female slaves ‘Father So-and-so, Mother So-and-so’. Those of the house of Rabban Gamaliel, however, were called ‘Father Ṭabi’ and ‘Mother Ṭabitha’.
We confine the term ‘our father’ to the three Patriarchs, and the term ‘our mother’ to the four Matriarchs.

We do not occupy ourselves in any respect with the funeral rites of one who committed suicide wilfully. R. Ishmael said: We exclaim over him, ‘Alas for a lost [life!] Alas for a [lost] life!’ R. ‘Aḳiba said to him, ‘Leave him unmourned; speak neither well nor ill of him’. We do not rend garments for him, bare the shoulder, or deliver a memorial address over him. We do, however, stand in a row for him and recite the benediction of mourners for him, from respect of the living [relatives]. The general rule is: With anything that makes for respect of the living we occupy ourselves, but with anything that does not make for the respect of the living, the public do not in any way occupy themselves.

Who [comes within the category of] ‘one who committed suicide wilfully’? He does not who climbed to the top of a tree and fell down and died, or he who went up to the top of the roof and fell down and died. But he who calls out, ‘Look, I am going to the top of the roof or to the top of the tree, and I will throw myself down that I may die’ [comes within the category]. When people saw him go up to the top of a tree or roof [for the purpose] and he fell down and died, he is presumed to have committed suicide wilfully; and with the person who commits suicide wilfully we do not occupy ourselves in any respect.
If a person was found strangled or hanging from a tree or lying dead on a sword, he is presumed not to have committed suicide wilfully, and none [of the rites] are withheld from him.

It is related of the son of Gorgias of Lydda that he ran away from school and his father pointed to his ear. In fear of his father he went and destroyed himself in a pit. They went and inquired of R. Ṭarfon who ruled: We do not withhold anything from him.

It is related of a child in Benë Beraḳ that he broke a bottle on the Sabbath and his father pointed to his ear. In fear of his father he went and destroyed himself in a pit. They inquired of R. ‘Aḳiba who ruled: We do not withhold anything from him.

Hence the Sages ruled: A man should not point at the ear of a child, but either punish him immediately or keep silent and say nothing to him. R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: With human nature, a child and a woman, the left hand should repulse them but the right hand bring them back.

With those executed by a Court we do not occupy ourselves in any respect. Their brothers and relatives come and greet the witnesses and judges [as if to say], ‘We have no [ill feelings] against you in our hearts because you gave a true judgment’. They observe no [public] mourning for them but grieve, since grief is felt only in the heart.
R. Nathan said: There is no difference between silence and mourning.

The ‘meal of comfort’ is not eaten in their case, as it is stated, Ye shall not eat [anything] with the blood . [The judges of] a Court who ordered the execution of a man used not to eat anything on that day. [The condemned] are allowed to converse with their brothers and relatives; and not to delay matters they are given to drink wine containing frankincense so that they should not feel grieved. They are urged to confess, because he who confesses has a portion in the World to Come. We find it so with Achan to whom Joshua said, My son, give, I pray thee, glory to the Lord, the God of Israel, and make confession unto Him; and tell me now what thou hast done; hide nothing from me. And Achan answered Joshua, and said: Of a truth I have sinned against the Lord, the God of Israel, and thus and thus have I done . What is the meaning of and thus and thus? It teaches that he violated the ban twice. [44 b ] I have sinned , i.e. I and not my household, I and not my children. This teaches that he truthfully confessed. And whence do we know that his confession made atonement for him? As it is stated, And Joshua said: Why hast thou troubled us? The Lord shall trouble thee this day — this day art thou to be troubled but thou shalt not be troubled in the World to Come; and it states, And the sons of Zerah: Zimri, and Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol and Dara: five of them in all. Do we not know that there were five of them in all? It teaches that Achan will be with them in the world to come. Similarly one who steals the tax or anything devoted [to the Sanctuary] is as if he shed blood; and not only is he as if he shed blood, but he is also as if he worships idols, was guilty of immorality and desecrates the Sabbath.

We do not occupy ourselves with those who separated themselves from the community in any respect. Their brothers and relatives clothe themselves in white, wrap themselves in white and eat and drink and rejoice because an enemy of the All-present perished; as it is stated, Do not I hate them, O Lord, that hate Thee? And do not I strive with those that rise up against Thee? I hate them with utmost hatred; I count them mine enemies .

We do not withhold mourning rites from those executed by the Government. When do we begin to count [the days of mourning] for them? From the time that [the relatives] despaired in their appeal [for the body to be delivered to them for burial], but not [given up the hope] of stealing it. For he who steals is as if he shed blood, and not only is he as if he had shed blood, but also as if he worshipped idols, etc.

Mourning rites are not withheld in any respect from one who fell into the sea, or was washed away by a stream, or killed by a wild beast. When do we begin to count [the days of mourning] for such as these? From the time that hope of finding them has been given up. If they found a body limb by limb, we do not count [the days of mourning] until the head and greater part [of the torso] is found. R. Judah said: The spine and skull constitute the greater part [of the torso].

If one’s husband, wife, father or mother had been impaled in his city, one should not continue to reside there unless it is a city as big as Antioch. [Even then] one should not reside in the same side of the city but in another part. Until when is one so forbidden? Until the flesh is completely decomposed and the identity unrecognizable from the bones.

[Beth Shammai said:] If a man divorced his wife, he should not live in the same alley or courtyard as she. If the alley belonged to both of them, he transfers the door [of his house] to another side; and if the courtyard belonged to both of them, one vacates it on account of the other, and the woman vacates it on account of the man. This rule only applies if she has remarried and in the case of the [divorced] wife of a kohen even if she has not remarried. It further applies only if she is divorced after marriage and not after betrothal. Likewise one who has freed his sister-in-law from the levirate marriage does not vacate on account of her, because he does not feel attracted to her.

A child who lived only one day counts to his father and mother as a fully-grown man. [The words] ‘who lived only one day’ are not to be taken as an [irreducible] limit; even if only his head and the greater part of his body came out viable [he is so counted, but in their formulation of the law] the Sages speak of what actually happens.

[An infant] who is carried in the arms is buried by one woman and two men. Abba Saul said: [The burial may be done] by one man and two women. [The Sages] said to him: One woman may be alone with two men, but one man may not be alone with two women. [The people at the burial] do not stand in line on account of him and they need not recite the mourner’s benediction on account of him unless he was thirty days old. If he was thirty days old, he is accompanied [to the grave] by men and women and is carried in a case upon the arms up to the age of twelve months. If he was twelve months old, he is accompanied by men and women and is carried in a case on the shoulder up to the age of three years. R. Judah said: Should his father desire to honour him, they take him out in a coffin to the cemetery even before he is three years old.

If three years old he is taken out on a bier. R. ‘Aḳiba said: If he is three years old but his limbs are [developed] like those of an infant two years old, or if he is two years old but his limbs are like those of an infant three years old, he is carried on a bier. Simeon the brother of Azariah said: For anyone who is taken out on a bier the people show their distress. R. Meir said in the name of R. Eleazar b. Azariah: If he is known to the public at large they participate in connection with him [at the funeral], but if not, they do not participate in connection with him.

R. Judah said in the name of R. Eleazar b. Azariah: For the purpose of a memorial address it is sufficient that his neighbours [know him]. In the case of the poor a memorial address is delivered for a child of three, and in the case of the rich for a child of four. R. ‘Aḳiba said: In the case of the poor, for a child of six and in the case of the rich for a child of seven. The children of the rich are like the children of scholars and the children of scholars like the children of kings.

In the case of a child of developed intelligence we dwell [in the memorial address for him] on his own [good] deeds, but if he has no such deeds we dwell on the deeds of his parents; and if his parents have no such deeds we dwell on the deeds of his relatives. In the case of a bride we dwell on the honour of her father or father-in-law, because she rises [in esteem] with him but does not fall with him. We may not ascribe merits to one who has none, but we may magnify those which he possessed.

In Jerusalem there was a saying, ‘Perform actions [which can be lamented] in front of your bier’, and in Judea there was a saying, ‘Perform actions [which can be lamented] behind your bier’. For in Jerusalem they recounted in front of a dead man’s bier only the merits which he possessed; but in Judea they recounted merits which he possessed and did not possess. They, however, who walked behind the bier only repeated after them the merits which he possessed. [One who dies] between the ages of three and thirty [is mourned] like a bridegroom; between thirty and forty like a brother; between forty and fifty like a father.

R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: Between thirty and forty, if he has children or the majority of his own age have children, [he is mourned] like a father; if not, like a brother. Between forty and fifty, if he has children or the majority of his own age have grandchildren, [he is mourned] like a grandfather, if not like a father.

If one dies under fifty, that is death by kareth; at fifty-two, that is the death of Samuel of Ramah; at sixty, that is the death referred to in the Torah, as it is stated, Thou shalt come to thy grave in ripe age; at seventy, that is the death of the hoary head, as it is stated, The days of our years are threescore years and ten; at eighty, that is the death of a vigorous old man, as it is stated, Or even by strength fourscore years . More than this is a life of trouble, for so Barzilai the Gileadite said to David, I am this day fourscore years old; can I discern between good and bad?

If one dies after [an illness of] one day, that is a death by [divine] wrath; after two days, it is a precipitous death; after three days, it is a death by pestilence; after four days, it is a hurried death; after six days, it is the death decreed in the Torah; after seven days, it is a death of [divine] love; after a longer period, it is a death of suffering.

R. Ḥanina b. Antigonos said: An old man who eats forbidden fat or one who desecrates the Sabbath dies by kareth . And what is there to show us that they died by kareth? But he who dies after [an illness of] three days dies by kareth; after four by a hurried death; after six, it is the death decreed in the Torah; after seven it is a death of [divine] love; after a longer period it is a death by suffering. R. Judah said: The pious men of former times used to suffer with stomach trouble for about twenty days before death in order to be cleansed of everything, so that they should come pure into the World to Come; as it is said, The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, and a man is tried by his praise . [45 a ].

For all [the nearest of kin] for whom a kohen defiles himself as commanded in the Torah [a mourner must observe mourning], viz. for his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, sister and wife. R. ‘Aḳiba said: For relatives in the second degree he observes the periods of mourning and grieves, [but should he be a kohen ] he does not defile himself.

R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: He mourns for his father’s father and son’s son. But the Sages said: For whomsoever he mourns he should mourn with, and for whomsoever he does not mourn, he does not mourn with. If there is a doubt whether [the deceased] is a brother or not or whether he is his son or not, he mourns and grieves for him, but [if he is a kohen ] he does not defile himself for him.
For his betrothed wife one does not mourn, grieve, or [if a kohen ] defile himself. For his divorced wife, although he had children by her, he does not mourn, grieve, or [if a kohen ] defile himself.

Which is [the period of] ‘grieving’? From the day of the death until the day of the burial, according to R. Meir; but the Sages said: ‘Grieving’ is only for one day. If a High Priest is married to a widow or an ordinary kohen to a divorced woman or one freed from levirate marriage, he mourns and grieves for her but does not defile himself.
For his betrothed sister, R. Meir said that [a kohen ] defiles himself. R. Judah and R. Simeon said that he does not.

For [his sister who was] ‘wounded’, R. Judah said that [a kohen ] defiles himself. R. Meir and R. Simeon said that he does not. For a woman who was raped or seduced, all agree that [a kohen ] does not defile himself. For an adolescent, all agree that he defiles himself.

The general principle laid down by R. Simeon is: He defiles himself for any one who is eligible [to marry] a High Priest, but may not defile himself for one who is not eligible [to marry] a High Priest.
Of all those regarding whom they said that a kohen defiles himself, the defilement is not voluntary but obligatory. R. Simeon said: It is voluntary. R. Joshua said: It is obligatory.

It is related of Joseph, a kohen , that his wife died on the eve of Passover and he would not defile himself for her. His colleagues pushed him and defiled him forcibly. Defilement is not voluntary but compulsory.

Until how long is it one’s duty to defile himself for her? R. Meir said: The whole of that day; R. Judah said: Up to three hours. R. Judah said in the name of R. Ṭarfon: Until the top stone closes the grave.

It is related that when R. Simeon b. Yehoẓadaḳ died in Lydda, his brother Joḥanan came from Galilee to defile himself for him after the top stone had closed the grave. They went and inquired of the Sages who said: He may not defile himself, but open the grave for him that he may view [the body].

It is related of a boy that he willed away his property to strangers and left his family out. They protested saying, ‘Let [his body] be examined’. They went and inquired of the Sages who said, ‘The body may not be examined; after the top stone has closed the grave, a corpse may not be moved from his place’. Another explanation is: Since he is dead, his hair has undergone change.

An ordinary kohen who defiled himself for his near kin may not defile himself for strangers even on the same day. This rule applies only when there are sufficient to carry the bier and bury him, but if there are not sufficient to carry the bier and bury him, then he must defile himself. Should he have defiled himself and sufficient people come to carry the bier and bury, he must withdraw to a place of cleanness.

Should there be two roads [for his return from the cemetery] one short but [ritually] unclean and one long but [ritually] clean, if the other persons take the longer road he should go with them; and if they do not, he should take the unclean road out of respect for the people.
While he stands and buries his dead he may, during the time he is standing in the grave, receive [a body] for burial from others; but once he has withdrawn from the grave he may not defile himself.

If he defiles himself [for a stranger] on the same day [as for another], R. Ṭarfon deems him culpable, but R. ‘Aḳiba frees him from culpability. If he defiles himself the next day, all are agreed that he is culpable, because he has rendered one day [of his mourning] void.

A kohen must defile himself for his near kin even when they have a disqualification; for his son and daughter who are Nethinim or illegitimate; for his brother and sister who are Nethinim or illegitimate; but not for any issue he may have from a slave or a non-Jewess (nor from the issue he may have from another source).
If there is a doubt whether [the deceased] is his brother or not or whether he is his son or not, he mourns and grieves but [if a kohen ] he does not defile himself.
How long is [the period of] ‘grieving’? From the day of the death until the day of the burial, according to the view of R. Meir; but the Sages said: ‘Grieving’ is for one day only.
A High Priest who defiles himself for the dead, lets the hair of his head go loose, or rends his garments, receives forty lashes.

Any defilement contracted by a Nazirite from the dead and for which he must shave his head, if contracted by a High Priest he receives forty lashes for it; but [for those defilements for which] the Nazirite has not to shave his head, [if contracted by a High Priest], he does not receive forty lashes.
A High Priest who defiles himself or enters a cemetery receives forty lashes.
If [a kohen ] entered the residence of non-Jews or the territory of Gentiles or a beth happeras or goes outside the land [of Israel], he receives punishment for disobedience.
If he enters a field wherein [the location of] a grave had disappeared, he is not culpable unless he traverses the whole of it.

A kohen may defile himself by going outside the land [of Israel] for the purpose of [dealing with a non-Jewish Court in] a civil suit or a capital charge, to announce the new moon or intercalate the year, or to rescue his field from a non-Jew, even if he only goes to protest [against his taking possession of it].

[He may go outside the land of Israel] to study Torah or to take a wife. R. Judah said: If he has nowhere else to study he may so defile himself, otherwise he may not. R. Jose said: Even though he has elsewhere to study he may defile himself, because no one is so meritorious as to be able to learn Torah from any man. It is related of Jose the Babylonian that he defiled himself by going outside the land [of Israel to study Torah] with R. Jose in Zidon.

A kohen must defile himself for [the burial of] a bone from his father’s [corpse] of the size of a barleycorn, but he may not defile himself for a limb severed from a living person be it even that of his father. R. Judah said: At first [a kohan ] may not defile himself for a limb severed from a corpse, be it even that of his father.

It is related of Joseph [the son of] Pisḳas who had a swelling on his foot that a doctor came to remove it. He said to him, ‘When you have left as much as a single hair, tell me’. He cut the abscess, and when he had left only as much as a single hair, he informed him. He called his son Neḥunia and said to him, ‘My son, until now it was your duty to attend to me, but now go your way; for the Sages said, “One must not defile himself for a limb that was severed from a living person, even if it be his father’s” ’. When the Sages heard of it they said, ‘Of such a man as he it has been stated, My soul is continually in my hand; yet have I not forgotten Thy law; [and it further states,] There is a righteous man that perisheth in his righteousness and there is a wicked man that prolongeth his life in his evil-doing.’

If he found a meth miẓwah , he must attend to him and bury him. Which is a meth miẓwah.? When [he who finds the body] cries out and the inhabitants of the city cannot hear his voice; but if they can hear his voice, it is not a meth miẓwah .
[The body remains] a meth miẓwah until sufficient people arrive to carry the bier and bury him; but once there are sufficient to carry the bier and bury him it is no longer a meth miẓwah . [45 b ]

If a High Priest and a Nazirite [found a meth miẓwah ], R. Eliezer said that the High Priest should defile himself and not the Nazirite, because the latter must offer a sacrifice on his defilement whereas the former does not. But the Sages said: The Nazirite should defile himself even if he has to bring a hundred sacrifices, and let not the High Priest defile himself, because the one is consecrated from the womb and the other is not, and the consecration of the one is temporary and that of the other permanent.

All are agreed that [in the case of the High] Priest anointed with the oil of anointing and [the High Priest robed] in many vestments, the latter must defile himself. As between a [High Priest robed] in many vestments and a deputy [High Priest] who had been anointed, the latter must defile himself. As between a deputy [High Priest] and a memunneh , the latter must defile himself. As between a memunneh and a kohen anointed for war, the latter must defile himself. As between a kohen anointed for war and an ordinary kohen , the latter must defile himself. As between an ordinary kohen and a Levite, the Levite must defile himself. As between a Levite and a lay-Israelite, the latter must defile himself. If, however, the two [who find a meth miẓwah ] are of equal status, the quicker of the two must defile himself; and if the two of them are [equally] quick, then whichever of them wishes to do so should defile himself.

If they found [the body] between a ploughed field and a fallow field, they bury him in the fallow field; between a ploughed field and a field sown with seeds, they bury him in the ploughed field; between a field sown with seeds and an orchard, they bury him in the field sown with seeds; between an orchard and a vineyard, they bury him in the orchard. If both are alike, they bury him in the nearer of the two; and if they are equidistant, they bury him in whichever of them they desire.

R. ‘Aḳiba said: This was the beginning of my ministration before the Sages. I once went out early and found the body of a man who had been killed. I took charge of him for a distance of three Sabbath-limits until I brought him to a place of burial and buried him. When I came and discussed the matter before the Sages, they said to me, ‘For each step you took it will be accounted to you as if you had committed murder’. I then argued from the less to the greater as a result of my experience: if when I intended to perform a meritorious act I rendered myself culpable, how much more so if I had not intended to perform a meritorious act!’ Whenever a person repeated this incident before R. ‘Aḳiba, he exclaimed, ‘This was the beginning of my ministration [before the Sages]’.

A mourner is forbidden to do work throughout the seven days [of mourning], he, his sons and daughters, his male and female slaves and his cattle; and as he is forbidden to do work, so too others are forbidden to do work for him.

They may do work for him in connection with perishable things; they may gather his harvest for him, operate his wine-press for him and bung his casks. If his olives had been turned, R. Judah says that he may put on the first beam and after his mourning he completes the work. R. Jose said to him, ‘But they are perishable things! He may complete [the whole operation in his mourning]’.

With regard to his flax [which is ready] for lifting from the retting and his wool [ready] for lifting from the dye-bath, if there are others [to do the work] they should lift it, but if not he may lift it in private.

If his cask [of wine] is [ready] for bunging, R. Judah says that they cover it with shingles and after the mourning he completes [the work]. R. Jose said to him, ‘But it is perishable ! He may complete [the whole operation in his mourning]’.

They may besprinkle his white field but may not sow it; they may sow for him a strip [of field] for a crop of flax when his turn for watering rights comes, according to R. Eliezer; but the Sages said: If he had not already sown it with flax, he should sow it with another kind [of crops], and if he does not sow it that week, he can sow it the following week.
If he is a baker in the town and there is no other, he may do the work in private out of respect for the public.
R. Simeon b. Yoḥai said: If he is a hair-dresser or a bath-attendant in the service of the public, and a Festival is close at hand, he may do the work in private out of respect for the public.

If he is engaged in cutting a person’s hair and people come and tell him, ‘Your father is dead’, he should complete the work; this applies whether he is the hair-dresser or he is having his hair dressed. Workmen who have undertaken to do work for a mourner are forbidden to do it in his house but may do it in their own. R. Simeon b. Yoḥai said: A workman hired by the day is forbidden to do work in either [place]; a workman on a contract basis is forbidden [to do it in the mourner’s] house, but may do it in his own home. If it is work in connection with objects attached to the ground, it is forbidden [to do the work in either place]; in another town it is permitted in either case.

A mourner overtaken by his days of mourning may ease [his hair] with a shearing-knife or a clipping-tool, but not with a scissors; and if his clothes are soiled he may wash them in cold water but not in urine.

A mourner and an excommunicated person who are travelling on the road are permitted to wear their shoes, but as soon as they reach a city they must remove them. The same rule applies [to everybody] on the Ninth of Ab and on a public fast day.

An excommunicated person who died has to be ‘stoned’—not that they place a high heap of stones upon him, as in the case of Achan—but the messenger of the Beth Din takes a stone and places it on the coffin in order to fulfil the duty of ‘stoning’ in his case.

An excommunicated person may not read a passage of Scripture to others nor may others read it to him; he may not teach nor may others teach him; but he may read Scripture and study for himself so as not to forget his learning.
He may be hired to work and others may hire themselves to him for work; not for his profit, but in order not to close the door before him.

One who is placed under excommunication by his city is not considered to be under it in another city; [46 a ] one under the ban to the disciples is not under the ban to the Sages; one under the ban to the Sages is under the ban to the disciples; one under the ban to all the people is not under the ban to the Nasi’; one under the ban to the Nasi’ is under the ban to all the people.
If one of those who had placed a person under the ban dies, should he have given authority to his colleagues [to annul the ban], they free him, otherwise they do not.
No ban holds for less than thirty days, and no ‘reproof’ for less than seven days.
Rabban Gamaliel said: Any one against whom the Sages pronounce excommunication, even if they later received him back, does not leave the world in peace.

A mourner is forbidden to read the Pentateuch, Prophets and Hagiographa; he is also forbidden to study Mishnah, Talmud, halakoth and ’aggadoth . He is under the prohibition to bathe, anoint [the body], put on sandals and cohabit. He is obliged to cover his head and overturn his couch. It is related of Rabban Gamaliel that when his wife died he bathed on the first night. His disciples said to him, ‘Master, have you not taught us that a mourner is forbidden to bathe?’ He replied, ‘I am not like other men, I am delicate’.

If people greet him, he should say to them, ‘I am a mourner’. On the first day and on the second day he should say to them, ‘I am a mourner’, but on the third day he may return their salutation in a low voice, although he may not greet them.

On the first day he does not put on the tefillin; on the second day he puts them on and if people come to comfort him he takes them off, according to the view of R. Eliezer. R. Joshua said: On the first and second day he does not put on the tefillin; on the third day he puts them on and if people come to comfort him he takes them off.

If [another] death took place in that city, on the first and second day [of his own mourning] he does not go out with [the other mourners], but on the third day he goes out with them and stands in the line to receive condolence but not to offer comfort to the others. This only holds good when there are sufficient people to carry the bier and do the burial, but if there are not sufficient he goes out with them even on the first day.

If he came from another district to his relatives, on the second and third day he completes [the days of his mourning] with them, but from the fourth day he counts [the remaining period of mourning] on his own. R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: If he found them still sitting [as mourners] even if it is the seventh day he completes [the period] with them; and if he did not find them sitting [as mourners] even if it be the second day he counts on his own.
On the first and second day, he may not do work even if he is in receipt of charity. On the third day he may work but in private.

He may not work in a field adjoining the city or the road, but he may work privately in his own garden. Likewise a woman may not work on top of the roof or within the courtyard, but she may work privately in her house so long as she is not overlooked by her neighbours.
[The period of] three days applies to a dog which devoured [some of] the flesh of a corpse and entered a house. If this happened after three days the house is clean, if less it is unclean.
[The period of] three days applies to any of the five species [of grain] sown; [if three days] before Passover it is permitted [to be eaten], if less than this it is prohibited.

One should not go out with a caravan less than three days before the Sabbath. One may not go out to war, if it is of a voluntary nature, less than three days before the Sabbath. One may not set out on a ship less than three days before the Sabbath.

On the first and second day [of mourning] he may not enter the Temple Mount; on the third day he may enter but must go round to the left. These are they who must go round to the left: a mourner, an excommunicated person, one who has a sick person in his house, and one who lost an object. [When asked,] ‘Why do you go round to the left?’ [he answers,] ‘Because I am a mourner’. They reply, ‘May He Who dwells in this House comfort you’. [If he says,] ‘Because I am under a ban’, [they reply,] ‘May He Who dwells in this House put it into their heart to draw you near’; so said R. Meir. R. Jose said to him, ‘You make out as if they [who banned] passed a wrong judgment on him; but [what they say is,] “May He Who dwells in this house put it into your heart to hearken to the words of your colleagues so that they may draw you near” ’. To one who has a sick person in his house they say, ‘May He Who dwells in this House have mercy upon him’; and if he is barely living [they say,] ‘May He have mercy upon him immediately’. It is related of a certain woman whose daughter was ill that she ascended the Temple Mount and went round it, and did not move from there until they came and told her, ‘She is cured’. To one who lost some object they say, ‘May He Who dwells in this House put it into the heart of the finder to return it to you at once’. It is related of Eleazar b. Ḥananiah b. Hezekiah b. Gorion that he lost a scroll of the Torah which he had bought for one hundred minas . He ascended [the Temple Mount], went round it and did not move from there until they came and told him, ‘The scroll of the Torah has been found’.

From the beginning Solomon built the Temple only on condition that anyone in trouble would come there and pray; as it is stated, If there be in the land famine, if there be pestilence, if there be blasting or mildew, locust or caterpillar; if their enemy besiege them in the land of their cities; whatsoever plague, whatsoever sickness there be; what prayer and supplication soever be made by any man . I have here only the case of an individual; whence do we know that it also holds good of a community? The text continues, Of all Thy people Israel . Whence do we know that it holds good of the non-Jew? The text states, Moreover concerning the stranger that is not of Thy people Israel . From the words be made by any man you might think that it holds good of one who wants children or possessions which will not be for his welfare; hence Scripture states, For Thou, even Thou only, knowest the hearts of all the children of men —what is good for him do Thou give to him. And whence do we know that this holds good only if they do not continue in their rebellion? As it is stated, Who shall know every man the plague of his own heart, and spread forth his hands toward this house .

The Sabbath enters into the number of the days of mourning but does not interrupt; Festivals interrupt but do not enter into the number. R. Eliezer said: Since the destruction of the Temple, ‘ Aẓereth is reckoned as the Sabbath [during the period of mourning]. Rabban Gamaliel said: New Year and the Day of Atonement are [in this respect] like the Festivals; but the Sages say: The rule is according to the view of neither, but ‘ Aẓereth is like the Festivals and the New Year and Day of Atonement are like the Sabbath.

If a man suffered a bereavement one day before a Festival, he interrupts [his mourning] throughout the Festival and counts six days [of mourning] after the Festival; if three days before the Festival he does not need to overturn his couch [after the Festival] according to R. Eliezer; but the Sages said: Even one day, or even one hour [before the Festival]. R. Eliezer b. R. Simeon said: These are the very words of Beth Shammai, and also the very words of Beth Hillel; because Beth Shammai said, ‘Three days before a Festival’ and Beth Hillel said, ‘Even one day and even one hour’. [46 b ]

Abba Saul said: If one buried his dead three days before a Festival, the restrictions appertaining to the seven days’ mourning cease to apply to him; if eight days before a Festival, the restrictions of the thirty days cease to apply (and the ruling is in accordance with this statement).

[Should the death occur] eight days before a Festival, if he wishes to cut his hair or wash his clothes on the eve of the Festival he may do so; if he did not cut his hair or wash his clothes on the eve of the Festival, he may not do so until the thirty days are completed.

[If the death occurs] two days within the Festival, he interrupts [the mourning] for all the Festival and counts seven [days] after it, and people occupy themselves with him for the five days after the Festival. [If the death occurs] seven days within the Festival, he interrupts [the mourning] for all the Festival and counts [seven days] after the Festival, and the community do not occupy themselves with him at all after the Festival.
On the days which he counts after a Festival, neither his slave nor his cattle need abstain from work; only he and his near kin conduct themselves like mourners.

A Festival is reckoned for the mourner into the count of the thirty [days] but not into the count of the seven [days]. A mourner is regarded on a Festival as if he were no mourner, but in matters of a private nature he does observe mourning. The general rule is: as regards any [mourning rite] in the carrying out of which others are associated with him, a Festival is taken into account with the seven days, otherwise it is not taken into account with them.

Thirty are the days of mourning. For thirty days he may not put on pressed clothes or cut his hair. Thirty days are allowed for the collection of debts; thirty days must elapse before a captive woman of ‘goodly form’ may be taken to wife; thirty days in the case of betrothal; thirty days in the case of marriage; thirty days within which a charge of lack of virginity can be made; thirty days are granted to a widow about to remarry to make her preparations; thirty days for a sister-in-law [after her levirate marriage to declare, ‘He has not cohabited with me’]. If a man forbade his wife by vow to have any benefit from him [the prohibition lasts] thirty days. The vow of a Nazirite of unspecified duration [remains in force] for thirty days.
Whence [thirty days] for mourning? As it is stated, And the children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days .

How is it with pressed clothes? It is forbidden [for a mourner] to don pressed clothes, i.e. those that came from the press. This is the view of Rabbi [Judah the Prince]; the Sages said: [It refers] to dyed but not white garments. R. Meir said: White but not dyed, new but not worn garments. He may put on his money-belt, girdle, felt-shoes and turban. It is permitted to take garments to be pressed within thirty days.

How is it with cutting the hair? [A mourner] is forbidden to remove the hair whether of the head or of his [upper] lip, or of the beard or of the hair on any part of him. A woman is permitted to remove hair after the seven days. How is it with the collection of debts? If a person lends his friend money without specifying a date [for repayment], he may not demand it of him until thirty days are completed.

How is it with a woman of ‘goodly form’? [It is stated,] And thou hast a desire unto her, and wouldest take her to thee to wife; then thou shalt bring her home to thy house; and she shall shave her head, and pare her nails . [This means that] she shall shave her head and cut her nails, so the view of R. Eliezer; R. ‘Aḳiba [takes the meaning to be,] she lets the hair of her head grow long and lets her nails grow. R. Eliezer said: An act is mentioned in respect of the head and an act is mentioned in respect of her nails; as the former signifies removal of the hair so the latter signifies removal of the nails. R. ‘Aḳiba said: An act is mentioned in respect of the head and an act is mentioned in respect of the nails; as disfigurement is the purpose of the former so is disfigurement the purpose of the latter. There is a support for R. Eliezer [in the verse], And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king; and he had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard . There is a support for R. ‘Aḳiba [in the verse], Till his hair was grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws . And she shall put the raiment of her captivity from off her . If she wore white garments and they were comely for her, black garments and they were comely for her, bracelets, nose-rings or rings, they are taken away from her so that she should sit and appear in her disfigurement. And she shall remain in thy house: so that while she remains in his house he enters and sees her in her disfigurement. And bewail her father and her mother: this means her actual father and mother, in the view of R. Eliezer; but R. ‘Aḳiba explains that her father and her mother refers to the idols [which she worshipped], as it is stated, Who say to a stock: ‘Thou art my father’, and to a stone: ‘Thou hast brought us forth’ . A month of days —i.e. thirty days. R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: [It means] three months, as it is stated, And bewail her father and her mother a month , i.e. one month, of days signifies [with the former] two months, and after that [is added in the text] to include the third month, [the purpose being] that the holy seed shall not be mingled with that of other peoples. When does this apply? Only if she does not wish to become a proselyte; but if she is willing to become a proselyte, he has her immersed [in the ritual bath] and emancipates her, and is permitted to marry her forthwith. R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: Even if she is not willing at first, he has her immersed as a handmaid, emancipates her and may marry her forthwith. Why all this [procedure]? In order that the holy seed should not be mingled with that of other peoples. It is better for Israelites to eat the flesh of animals about to die, yet ritually slaughtered, than the flesh of dying animals which definitely perished.
How is it with betrothal? It is forbidden to hold a betrothal feast within the thirty days [of mourning].

How is it with marriage? It is forbidden to hold a marriage feast within the thirty days [of mourning], but if his meat is prepared and his father or mother-in-law died, he brings the bride into the bridal chamber, performs the act of consummation and then separates himself from her [until] after the seven days. When does this apply? Only if his father or mother-in-law died; but if his wife died, he is forbidden to remarry until three Festivals have gone by. R. Judah said: Until two Festivals have gone by, and he brings [her into the marital chamber] on the third. When does this apply? Only if he has children, but if he has no children or his children are young, it is permitted for him to remarry within thirty days. It happened that R. Ṭarfon’s wife died, and he said to her sister within the days of mourning, ‘Be my wife and bring up your sister’s children’. Nevertheless he did not cohabit with her until after the thirty days.
How is it with virginity? Within thirty days he may make a plea of the absence of virginity, but after thirty days he cannot.

How is it with a widow? If the man [to whom she is betrothed] claims her [in marriage] and she holds back, we allow her thirty days to make provision for herself; and as we allow [that period] to the woman, so too we allow it to the man.

How is it with a sister-in-law? If a sister-in-law declared within thirty days [after the levirate marriage], ‘I have had no cohabitation’, [the levir] is compelled to give her ḥaliẓah , but [if her declaration was made] after thirty days, he is not compelled to give her ḥaliẓah .

Should a man forbid his wife by vow to have any benefit from him, [if the prohibition is to last] not more than thirty days he must appoint a steward, but if for a longer period he must divorce her and give her [the amount stipulated in] her kethubah .

[How is it with a Nazirite whose vow is of unspecified duration?] The vow of a Nazirite which is of unspecified duration [remains in force] thirty days. Whether he declared, ‘Behold I am a Nazirite’ without qualification, or he declared, ‘Behold I am a Nazirite for one day’, his status as a Nazirite lasts thirty days. If he completed his period as a Nazirite outside the land of Israel and later returned there, [47 a ] Beth Shammai said that he remains a Nazirite for thirty days, and Beth Hillel said that he [reverts to the] beginning of his status as a Nazirite.

One who resides in the land of Israel thirty days is under the obligation to affix a mezuzah , and he who rents a house must do so forthwith; but he who resides outside the land of Israel is exempt. One who rents a house for thirty days and one who resides in an isolated place for thirty days is under the obligation to affix a mezuzah .

If one buys newly born cattle from his neighbour, [he may retain the dam] to suckle them, in the case of small cattle for thirty days and in the case of large cattle for fifty days. R. Jose said: In the case of small cattle for three months because they need much attention. As for attending to the first-born of cattle [before handing them over to the kohen ], in the case of small cattle the period is thirty days and for large cattle fifty days. R. Jose said: In the case of small cattle the period is three months because they need much attention.

Beth Shammai declared an old Sukkah to be invalid; Beth Hillel pronounced it valid (but he must add something new to it). What is ‘an old Sukkah’? One which was made thirty days before the Festival [of Tabernacles]; but should he have made it for the purpose of [being used on] the Festival, even [if erected] at the beginning of the year, it is valid.

Rice, millet, panic and sesame which took root before the New Year are tithed as belonging to the previous year and are permitted in the seventh year; but if they did not [take root before the New Year] they are forbidden in the seventh year and are tithed as belonging to the next year. R. Simeon of Shezur said: Egyptian beans sown from the outset for the purpose of seeds are treated in a like manner. R. Simeon said: Large beans are treated in a like manner if they formed pods before the New Year. Shallots and Egyptian beans which have not been watered within thirty days of the New Year are treated as if a year had passed and may be retained in the seventh year; otherwise they are not considered as such and may not be retained in the seventh year.

If one plants, bends over or grafts a tree within thirty days of the New Year, a year has passed for him [by the New Year] and he may preserve the growth during the seventh year; otherwise a year has not passed for him and he may not preserve the growth in the seventh year. R. Judah said: Any grafting which does not take root within three days will never do so. R. Simeon and R. Jose said: Any grafting which does not take root within two weeks is no grafting. The fruit of such a planting is forbidden until the fifteenth of Shebaṭ .

We go out to the cemetery and examine the dead within three days and do not fear [being suspected of] superstitious practices. It once happened that [a man who was buried] was examined [and found to be living], and he lived for twenty-five years and then died. Another [so examined lived and] begat five children before he died.

We erect a canopy for bridegrooms and brides [who died before marriage] and suspend from it articles which have and have not reached the edible stage; this is the opinion of R. Meir. R. Judah said: We only suspend from it articles which have not reached the edible stage. These are what are suspended from it: Nuts which have not reached the edible stage, loaves of bread which are not edible, strips of purple wool, flasks of perfumed oil. And these are the articles which may not be suspended from it: Nuts which have reached the edible stage, pomegranates which have reached the edible stage, loaves of bread which are edible, and flasks of sweet oil. The general rule is: no benefit may be derived from anything that is suspended from the canopy.

We scatter before bridegrooms and brides strings of fish and pieces of meat in summer but not in winter; but not pieces of cooked fish, mushrooms, truffles or sesame both in summer and winter; but one takes roasted ears of corn and nuts and throws them. The general rule is: we may not scatter before them anything that is perishable.

We may let wine and oil flow through pipes before bridegrooms and brides and we do not fear [being suspected of] superstitious practices; nor do we fear of sinning by putting food to shame. It is related that Judah and Hillel, the sons of Rabban Gamaliel, came to Ben Zakkai at Kabul and the citizens let wine and oil flow through pipes [in their honour].

We may burn [articles] at the funerals of kings and mutilate [their animals], and we do not fear [being suspected of] superstitious practices. Any mutilation which disqualifies the animal as food makes it forbidden to be eaten, but benefit may be derived from it; and when the mutilation does not disqualify the animal it may be eaten and obviously benefit may be derived from it. Which mutilation disqualifies it? From the knee downwards.

We may burn articles at the funeral of kings but not at the funeral of princes. When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder died, the proselyte Onḳelos burnt after him more than eighty Tyrian minas . They asked him, ‘What was your purpose in doing this?’ He replied, ‘It is written, Thou shalt die in peace; and with the burnings of thy fathers, the former kings that were before thee, so shall they make a burning for thee . And is not Rabban Gamaliel worth more than a hundred useless kings?’

We cover the hair of [dead] brides, uncover the face of [dead] bridegrooms, and place ink and pen at their side, and we do not fear [being suspected of] superstitious practices. (When Rabban Gamaliel the Elder entered [the meeting place of the Rabbis to intercalate the year], he found eight [present]. He asked, ‘Who is it that entered without permission?’ Samuel the Small arose and said, ‘Rabbi, I entered only to inquire about the law [of intercalation]’. He answered, ‘O Eldad and Medad, all Israel know that if I had ordered that only two should enter, you would have been one [of them] to enter’.) We suspend the key and writing-tablet of a dead man from his coffin from grief of soul. When Samuel the Small died, they suspended his key and writing-tablet from his coffin because he had no son, and when Rabban Gamaliel the Elder and R. Eleazar delivered their funeral orations over him, they exclaimed, ‘For this one it is fitting to weep, for this one it is fitting to mourn. When kings die they leave their crowns to their sons; when wealthy men die they leave their riches to their children; but Samuel the Small has taken away with him all the desirable things in the world and has departed’. And thus he spoke at the time of his death, ‘Simeon [b. Gamaliel] and Ishmael [the son of Elisha the High Priest] are destined for the sword and the rest of the people for spoliation; great distress will befall [Israel] after them’. He uttered these words in Aramaic.

When R. Simeon b. Gamaliel and R. Ishmael came [to be tried], it was decreed against them that they should be put to death. Whereupon R. Ishmael broke into tears; and R. Simeon said to him, ‘ Abrek , why do you weep? Two steps more and you will be in the bosom of the righteous, and yet you weep!’ He replied, ‘Do I then weep because we are about to be executed? It is because we are about to be executed [in the same way] as murderers and desecrators of the Sabbath’. He said to him, ‘Perhaps you were having a meal or you were sleeping when a woman came to ask [a ruling] concerning her ritual impurity or her cleanness, and your servant told her that you were asleep. And the Torah states, Ye shall not aflict any widow or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise — for if they cry at all unto Me, I will surely hear their cry . And what is written after this? My wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword ’. Some say that it was [47 b ] R. Simeon b. Gamaliel who was weeping and R. Ishmael who answered him in these words. When R. Simeon and R. Ishmael were executed and the report reached R. ‘Aḳiba and R. Judah b. Baba, they arose, girded their loins with sackcloth, rent their garments and exclaimed, ‘Our brother-Israelites, if good were destined to come to the world, at first none would receive it but R. Simeon and R. Ishmael; but now that it is revealed before Him Who spake and the universe came into being that eventually great punishments will come upon the world, they have consequently been taken out of the world; [as it is stated,] The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart , and it continues, He entereth into peace, they rest in their beds ’.

When R. ‘Aḳiba was executed in Caesarea and the news reached R. Judah b. Baba and R. Ḥanina b. Teradion, they arose, girded themselves in sackcloth, rent their garments and exclaimed, ‘Our brethren, hearken unto us! R. ‘Aḳiba was not executed for robbery or because he did not labour in the Torah with all his strength. He has only been put to death as a sign, as it is stated, Thus shall Ezekiel be unto you a sign; according to all that he hath done shall ye do; when this cometh, then shall ye know that I am the Lord God . Within a short while there will be no place found in the land of Israel where no [slain] will be cast forth, as it is stated, Speak: Thus saith the Lord — And the carcasses of men fall as dung upon the open field, and as the handful after the harvestman, which none gathereth’ . It is reported that it was not long before war came and disturbed the world, and within twelve months the municipalities in Judea ceased; as it is stated, Tremble, ye women that are at ease; be troubled, ye confident ones: Ye women that are at ease refers to the municipalities in Judea, ye confident ones refers to the fortified towns. Confident ones is nothing else than a term for walled cities. It is reported that twelve months had not passed before what had been said was fulfilled.

R. Meir illustrated it by a parable. To what is the matter like? To a king who prepared a banquet and invited guests without fixing a time when they should leave. The shrewd among them left at the ninth hour, returned home and went to bed while it was still light; others left at sunset while the shops were still open and the lamps burning, entered their homes and went to bed by the light of the lamps; still others left at two or three hours in the night when some shops were open and some shut, some with their lamps alight and some with their lamps extinguished, entered their homes and went to bed in the dark. Those remaining at the banquet became intoxicated, and wounded and killed each other; as it is stated, I saw the Lord standing beside the altar; and He said: Smite the capitals, that the posts may shake; and break them in pieces on the head of all of them; and I will slay the residue of them with the sword .

When R. Ḥanina b. Teradion was arrested on the charge of heresy, [the Romans] sentenced him to be burnt, his wife to be executed and his daughter to be consigned to a brothel. He asked, ‘What have they decreed against that poor woman?’ They replied, ‘She is to be executed’. Thereupon he recited of her the verse, The Lord is righteous in all his ways . She asked, ‘What have they decreed against the Rabbi?’ They replied, ‘He is to be burnt’. Thereupon she recited of him the verse, Great in counsel, and mighty in work . When they burnt him, they wrapped him in a scroll of the Torah and burnt him. His daughter wept, wailed and threw herself before him. Whereupon he exclaimed, ‘My daughter, if for me you weep, if for me you throw yourself down, it were better that a fire which [a man] has fanned should consume me and not one which [a man] has not fanned; as it is stated, A fire not blown by man shall consume him . If, however, you threw yourself down because of the scroll of the Torah, behold, the letters are flying upwards and only parchment is being consumed. For even great servants of the king are punished by inferior servants, [as it is stated,] Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets, I have slain them by the words of My mouth’ .

R. ‘Aḳiba said: A king had four sons. One was silent when punished, another protested when punished, another begged for mercy when punished, and another when punished said to his father, ‘Go on punishing me’. Abraham remained silent when punished, as it is stated, Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac … and offer him there for a burnt-offering . He could have argued, ‘Yesterday You said to me, For in Isaac shall seed be called to thee! ’ Then it is stated, And Abraham rose early in the morning . Job protested when punished, as it is stated, I will say unto God: Do not condemn me; make me know wherefore Thou contendest with me . Hezekiah besought God for mercy when punished, as it is stated, Then he turned his face to the wall, and prayed unto the Lord, saying , etc. Some say that Hezekiah protested when he was punished since he later added, And have done that which is good in Thy sight . David [when punished] said to his Father, ‘Continue to punish me’, as it is stated, Wash me thoroughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin .

We do not interrupt the study of the Torah until the soul departs from the dying man. When R. Simeon, the son of R. ‘Aḳiba, fell ill, the latter did not interrupt his expositions in the Academy but made inquiries after him through a messenger. The first messenger came and reported, ‘He is very ill’. He said to [his disciples], ‘Continue to ask questions’. Then a second came and reported, ‘He has grown worse’. R. ‘Aḳiba resumed the study of the Torah. A third came and reported, ‘He is dying’, and he said [to his disciples, ‘Continue] to ask questions’. A fourth came and reported, ‘He is dead’. Whereupon he arose, removed the tefillin , rent his garments and said to them, ‘Our brother-Israelites, hearken! Until now we had the duty to study the Torah; but from now onward we have the duty to occupy ourselves with honouring the dead’. A large assembly gathered to bury R. ‘Aḳiba’s son, and he said to them, ‘Bring a bench for me to the cemetery’. He stood upon it and expounded, ‘Our brother-Israelites, hearken! Not because I am a scholar [have you come here], there being greater scholars here than I; not because I am a rich man [have you come here], there being richer men here than I; the men of the Darom know R. ‘Aḳiba, but how should the men of Galilee know him? Men know him, but how should women and young children? I know, however, that your reward is great because you have only taken the great trouble to come here for the honour of the Torah and for the sake of the commandment [to attend the dead to the grave]. I should be comforted though I had seven sons whom I [now] buried. Not that a man desires to bury his children, but I know that my son is destined for the World to Come because he caused the many to be righteous, and whoever causes the many to be righteous, sin occurs not through him, and whoever causes the many to sin, they do not afford him the faculty to repent. Moses was righteous and caused the many to be righteous, [therefore] the righteousness of the many was [considered] dependent on him, as it is stated, He executed the righteousness of the Lord, and His ordinances with Israel . Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, sinned and caused others to sin, [therefore] the sin of the many was [considered] dependent on him, as it is stated, For the sins of Jeroboam which he sinned, and wherewith he made Israel to sin’ .

Further [R. ‘Aḳiba] sat on the bench [and taught]: Good things are brought about through the agency of good men. Even if Moses and Aaron had not arisen, Israel would still have been worthy to be redeemed from Egypt, as it is stated, And afterward shall they come out with great substance . Had not Moses and Aaron and the Generation of the Wilderness arisen, Israel would still have been worthy to receive the Torah, as it is stated, He layeth up sound wisdom for the upright . The section of ‘the judges’ would have been worthy to be promulgated even if Jethro had not arisen. The section of ‘the smaller Passover’ would have been worthy to be promulgated even if the ‘unclean’ had not arisen, as it is stated, We are unclean by the dead body of a man; wherefore are we to be kept back, so as not to bring the offering of the Lord in its appointed season among the children of Israel? The section of ‘inheritance’ would have been worthy to be promulgated even if the daughters of Zelophehad had not arisen. The Temple would have been worthy to be built even if David and Solomon had not arisen, as it is stated, The sanctuary, O Lord, which Thy hands have established . Israel would have been worthy to be redeemed in the days of Haman even it Mordecai and Esther had not arisen, as it is stated, And yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly , etc. Israel were destined to be enslaved even if Pharaoh had not arisen in Egypt, as it is stated, And [they] shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years . Israel were destined to serve idols even if Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, had not arisen, as it is stated, And this people will rise up, and go astray after the foreign gods of the land . The section of ‘the blasphemer’ and of ‘the gatherer of sticks’ would have been worthy to be promulgated even if the son of the Israelitish woman and the gatherer of sticks had not arisen. Israel would have been destined to be destroyed by the sword even if so and so had not arisen, as it is stated, All the sinners of My people shall die by the sword; and it declares, By sword and famine shall they be consumed . Israel would have deserved to be destroyed even if Nebuchadnezzar and his companions had not arisen, as it is stated, Therefore shall Zion for your sake be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest .

And further [he expounded]: Reward is brought about through persons of merit and punishment through persons of guilt. When Trajan was about to execute Pappus and his brother Lulianus in Laodicea, he said to them, ‘If you are of the people of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, let your God come and deliver you from my hands, in the same way as He delivered Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah [from Nebuchadnezzar]’. They replied, ‘Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were worthy men and Nebuchadnezzar was a worthy king, and it was fitting that a miracle should be wrought through their agency; but you are a wicked king and are not worthy that a miracle should be wrought through your agency. As for us, we deserve death at the hand of God, and if you do not slay us, the Omnipresent has many other agents of death; He has many demons, many bears, many leopards, many snakes, many venomous serpents, many scorpions which will come and attack us; but when we die you will learn that we are the descendants of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah’. It is reported that before they died they witnessed his eyes gouged out.

The allegorical interpreters of Scripture said: And ye shall break down their altars: wherein have the trees and the stones sinned? Because they were a stumbling-block to man Scripture decreed, And ye shall break down . This is an argument from minor to major: if with trees and stones, which are capable neither of merit nor guilt, neither of good nor evil, because they were a stumbling-block to man the Torah declared, And ye shall break down , how much more [will a man be punished] who causes his neighbour to sin and turns him away from the way of life to the path of death! Similarly, And if a woman approach unto any beast, and lie down thereto, thou shalt kill the woman, and the beast . If a human being sinned, how has the animal offended? Because evil came to a human being through it, and so that the animal shall not pass through the street and people say, ‘This is the animal on account of which So-and-so was stoned’. This is an argument from minor to major: if with an animal, which is capable neither of merit nor guilt, neither of good nor evil, because it was a stumbling-block to a human being the Torah declared, It shall be stoned , how much more [will a man be punished] who causes his neighbour to sin and turns him from the way of life to the path of death! Similarly Scripture declares of the stones of the altar, Thou shalt lift up no iron tool upon them , and elsewhere it states, For if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast profaned it . Wherein is iron different from all other metals to be unfit for [the building of] the altar? Because the sword is a symbol of curse and the altar an agent of atonement; so we remove the symbol of curse on account of the agent of atonement. This is an argument from minor to major: if with the stones of the altar which do not see and speak, eat or drink, because they make peace between Israel and their Father in heaven the Torah declared, Thou shalt lift no iron tool upon them , the children of the Torah, who are an atonement for the world, how much more [should they not lift an iron tool against each other!] Similarly Scripture declares, Thou shalt build the altar of the Lord thy God of unhewn stones —stones that bring peace to the world. This is an argument from minor to major: if with stones which do not see or hear, speak or eat or drink, because they make peace between Israel and their Father in heaven they must be ‘whole’ [48 a ] before [the Holy One, blessed be He], how much more the children of the Torah, who are an atonement for the world, must be ‘whole’ before the Holy One, blessed be He!

One does not rend [his garments] for the dead except for his teacher who taught him wisdom. R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: When a Sage dies, all present at his death rend [their garments] for him, but all those who are not present do not rend them.

For a Sage who died one bares the right [shoulder]; for an ’Ab Beth Din who died one bares the left [shoulder]; for a Nasi’ who died one bares both shoulders. It is related that when R. Eliezer died, R. ‘Aḳiba bared both shoulders and kept on beating his heart until the blood flowed, and he cried out, ‘My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and the horsemen thereof! ’

One does not bare [the shoulder] for the dead in general but only for his father and mother; and if they are not worthy, he does not rend even for his father and mother. It is related that when R. ‘Aḳiba’s father died, those present bared [the shoulder], but he did not.
For the dead in general one rends [the garments] with a knife, but for his father and mother he does not rend with a knife.
For the dead in general one does not bare his chest, but for his father and mother he bares it.

For the dead in general one does not divide the [upper] selvage-border [of his garment], but for his father and mother he does divide it. R. Judah said: Any rending [of a garment] which does not divide the selvage-border is mere make-believe. R. Judah said: Any initial rending must be [to the extent of] three fingers, while the extension may be as small as he cares. One only rends as far down as the region of the navel. In the case of children, others rend for them. One who rends [not as a relative but] from respect [for the dead] may stitch [the edges] forthwith. The rending of one’s undershirt is not indispensable. R. Benjamin said in the name of R. ‘Aḳiba: One must rend the undershirt.

For the dead in general one rends only the uppermost [garment], but for his father and mother he must rend [all] even though he be wearing a hundred. A woman only rends her uppermost [garment]. R. Judah said: A woman rends her undergarment, turns it front to back, and then rends the remaining [garments].

For the dead generally one tacks the rent together after seven days, and [completely] restitches [the edges] after thirty; but for one’s father and mother one never restitches [the edges]. A woman tacks the rent together after seven [days] and restitches [the edges] after thirty. R. Judah said: A woman tacks the rent together immediately and restitches [the edges] after seven [days].

For the dead generally one expedites the bier and does not occupy himself unduly with their affairs; but in the case of his father and mother, whoever greatly occupies himself with their affairs and does not expedite the bier is praiseworthy. But if time is pressing, or the Sabbath-eve is approaching, or rain falls, he may expedite the bier for his father and mother and does not unduly occupy himself with their affairs.

For the dead in general it is forbidden to wear pressed clothes until thirty days [are completed], but in the case of his father and mother it is forbidden until the [next] Festival occurs and then only if his companions rebuke him.
For the dead generally it is forbidden to trim one’s hair until thirty days are completed; but in the case of his father and mother, one lets the hair grow long until his companions rebuke him.
For the dead generally one is forbidden to engage in trade until thirty days are completed; but for one’s father and mother until his companions rebuke him and say to him, ‘Come out with us’.
For the dead generally it is forbidden to go to a house of feasting until thirty days are completed; but for one’s father and mother, all the twelve months unless it is for a sacred cause.

If news reached him that his father died and he rent, but [in fact] it was his mother, he has done his duty. [If news reached him that] his mother died, but it was his father and he rent, he has done his duty. [If news reached him that] his father died and he rent, but it was one of his near relatives, he has done his duty. [If news reached him that] one of his near relatives died, but it was his father, he has not done his duty.

If one’s father and mother died [at the same time], he makes only one rent for the two of them. R. Judah b. Tema said: He rends for each separately. If one’s ten children died at the same time, he makes one rent for all of them. If after he had made a rent [for another] news reached him that his son died, he continues to rend until it [reaches down] to the navel; when it has reached the navel he turns [the garment] front to back. If his son died and he rent [and news of another death reached him], he leaves a space of three fingers and again rends.

The rent must be made only between the two borders; one who makes the rent along the border or at the side has not done his duty. R. Judah said: He has done his duty. R. Judah said: It happened in the days of Ḥarsum that people used to make the rent at the lower end [of the garment] and at the side. His colleagues retorted, ‘No proof may be adduced [from a practice adopted] in a time of danger’. A man dressed in torn garments does not rend. R. Judah said: One who rends a cloak of Birrus , a Brundisian cloak, a Poenula , a stitched garment or a veil, has not done his duty. One who rends a basted garment has done his duty. What constitutes a basted garment? [When its tear] has been completely basted.

These are the rents which may not be basted: [When it was done] for his father or mother, for his teacher who instructed him in wisdom, for a scroll of the Torah which has been burnt, for the ruined Temple, for evil tidings, [on hearing] the Divine Name blasphemed, on seeing Jerusalem from Mount Scopus, and [on the death of] a Nasi ’. Some add: [On the death of] a High Priest, a prophet, or an ’Ab Beth Din . As regards the burning of a scroll of the Torah, [the garment is rent] not on hearing of this happening but only when he stands by while it burns. As for the ruined Temple, [he rends his garment] even if he heard that it has been destroyed; similarly with evil tidings because they are as grievous as the destruction of the Temple. One who sees Jerusalem from Mount Scopus must rend; when he enters [the city] he extends the rent, and if he goes up [again to Jerusalem] he must extend it further. ‘If he goes up again’—this is to teach that he is obliged to make a rent every time he goes up [to Jerusalem] during each period [of thirty days]. If he came up [to Jerusalem] and settled there, he rends once and has thereby done his duty.

One who buys a tunic which has been rent [by a mourner] from his companion may not baste it unless he knows that the rent is of the kind which may be basted. One who sells a tunic which has been rent [by a mourner] to his companion must inform him whether the rent is of the kind which may be basted or not. All rent [garments] which may not be basted must not be sold to non-Jews or stitched together or be reversed from top to bottom, according to the view of R. Simeon; but R. Eliezer permits it to be done. One who borrows a tunic from his companion to go and visit his father and when he arrives finds that his father died, he rends it, bastes it and returns it to his companion. If, however, he borrowed it without specifying for what purpose he needed it, he is not permitted to rend it.

One who goes out before the bier of the dead with a garment already rent robs the dead [of his due]. More grievous is the robbing of the dead than robbing the living, because one who robs the living can appease him by making restitution, but one who robs the dead cannot appease him by making restitution. Likewise you may say: One who honours his father and mother after their death is as if he honoured them in their lifetime, since one who honours them while they are alive may do so from fear or for the sake of an inheritance; but he who honours them after their death does so in the name of Heaven only. He who made a rent for one [presumed] dead and he revived, if he dies immediately afterwards [the man who made a rent] has fulfilled his duty, but if [death occurred] after some time he has not done his duty.

Whosoever rescues garments from the dead robs the dead. There are times when a man may rescue them and times when he may not. [48 b ] If the garments have not touched the bier he may rescue them, but if they have touched the bier he may not. We, however, instruct people not to seize them. And whoever piles up garments on the dead commits a transgression because of the law which forbids wilful destruction, according to the view of R. Meir. R. Eliezer b. Ẓadoḳ said: It disgraces him. Rabban Gamaliel said: He causes maggots to breed upon [the dead]. R. Nathan said: The garment which goes down with him to the grave will come back with him in the time to come, as it is stated, It is changed as clay under the seal; and they stand as a garment .

A mourner, as long as his dead is lying before him, is exempt from reading the Shema‘ and Tefillah and from all the commandments prescribed in the Torah. Even if he desires to place himself under greater restrictions [than the law requires] he should not do so out of respect for the dead.

When the time comes for reading the Shema‘ , all the people [present] read it but he remains silent; when they stand to read the Tefillah , all read it but he justifies for himself the divine decree. What does he say? ‘Sovereign of all the universe, I have sinned before Thee; I have repaid but few of my obligations; I merit much more punishment than this; may it be Thy will to repair our breaches and to comfort us’. R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: He also prays for all the needs of the dead person.

A mourner eats [his meal] in the house of his neighbour, and if he has no neighbour he eats it in another room; and if he has no other room [than that in which the dead is lying], he puts up a partition and eats; and if he is not able to put up a partition, he turns his face away from the dead and eats. But he must not eat in a reclining posture, eat as much food as he needs, eat meat or drink wine. He is not included in the Zimmun , others do not say Grace on his behalf, and we do not request him, ‘Say Grace’. When does this apply? On week-days, but on the Sabbath he eats as much as he needs, he may eat meat and drink wine, and is included in the Zimmun . Rabban Gamaliel said: A mourner [is regarded] on the Sabbath as if he were not a mourner.
We do not remove the body [for burial] near [the time of] reading the Shema‘ , unless it is an hour before.

Once the bearers of the bier have carried [the body] out—such as are before the bier and such as are behind it—those who are before the bier, whose services are still needed, are exempt from reading the Shema‘ and are forbidden to wear shoes. All alike are exempt from the Tefillah and from putting on the tefillin .

Having buried the dead and returned [from the graveside], if they are able to begin and complete [the reading of the Shema‘ ] before arriving at the row, they read it and afterwards stand in the row; but if not, they stand in the row and afterwards read [the Shema‘ ] and the Tefillah .

The inner row [of the comforters] who can see the mourners is exempt [from reading the Shema‘ ], but the outer row is under the obligation. R. Judah said: Even if there be [only] one row, those who stand for the sake of [comforting] the mourner are exempt, but those who stand for the sake of [their own] honour [are under the obligation]. If they came to the memorial address, those who can see the mourners are exempt and those who cannot see them are under the obligation.

R. Simeon b. Eleazar said: Rabban Gamaliel had a borrowed grave in Jabneh where they brought the dead and locked the door behind it. Men came, stood in the row and comforted the mourners and the public was thereby exempt [from this duty]. Later [the bodies] were conveyed to Jerusalem [for burial].
